title: THE FORGOTTEN MAN WHO HELD THE PEN WHEN GOD GAVE THE WORLD ROMANS
paragraphs: THE FORGOTTEN MAN WHO HELD THE PEN WHEN GOD GAVE THE WORLD ROMANS

His name appears only once in Scripture. He wasn't the apostle. He wasn't the preacher. But hidden inside one of Christianity's most powerful letters is a man whose quiet service still speaks to every believer who has ever wondered, “Does what I do for God really matter?”
There is a man in your Bible whom millions of Christians have read past without ever noticing.
He wasn't one of the Twelve.
He didn't walk on water. He didn't raise the dead. Scripture records no sermon he preached, no miracle he performed, and no church he planted.
Yet his handwriting may have carried some of the most extraordinary words about sin, judgment, mercy, justification, and salvation ever written.
Words that would confront generations of sinners.
Words that would comfort the brokenhearted.
Words that would help shape centuries of Christian theology.
Words that would explain how a holy God can declare guilty people righteous without compromising His justice.
And near the end of that remarkable letter, almost as though someone briefly stepped out from behind the curtain, a man introduced himself.
“I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord.” — Romans 16:22 (KJV)
Read that again.
“I Tertius…”
Not Paul.
Tertius.
Wait.
If Paul wrote Romans, why does another man say he wrote it?
And why would God preserve the name of someone most Christians would never remember?
The answer is more beautiful than a historical curiosity.

Because somewhere in this forgotten man's story is a truth for the mother who serves without recognition, the father who works until his hands ache, the believer who quietly supports ministry, the volunteer nobody thanks, and the Christian who sometimes wonders whether heaven notices the little things.
But before we get to that, we need to understand what actually happened.
The Letter to the Romans is rightly attributed to the apostle Paul.
Romans 1:1 identifies him as its sender: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God.”
And yet Romans 16:22 reveals that Tertius was the one who physically wrote the letter.
There is no contradiction.
In the ancient world, writers commonly employed a secretary, sometimes called an amanuensis, to record correspondence.
Paul was the author of Romans. Tertius was its scribe.
Paul was responsible for the apostolic message. Tertius helped put that message into written form.
The distinction matters.
Tertius was not secretly the theological author of Romans. We have no evidence that he invented Paul's arguments, supplied the doctrine of justification, or independently composed the letter.
Nor does Scripture tell us precisely whether Paul dictated every word, worked from prepared material, or allowed his scribe some limited freedom in expression.
What we do know is enough.
Tertius served in the production of a letter that would outlive both men.
And he left behind one sentence that has survived nearly two thousand years.
The original Greek makes the moment even more striking.
Romans 16:22 reads:
Ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ Τέρτιος ὁ γράψας τὴν ἐπιστολὴν ἐν κυρίῳ.
Transliteration:
Aspazomai hymas egō Tertios ho grapsas tēn epistolēn en kyriō.
A close translation is:
“I, Tertius, the one who wrote the letter, greet you in the Lord.”
Notice the phrase ὁ γράψας τὴν ἐπιστολήν (ho grapsas tēn epistolēn).
It means “the one who wrote the letter.”
Here, the natural understanding is that Tertius performed the physical writing.
But something else deserves attention.
He did not merely say, “I wrote this.”
He said, “I greet you in the Lord.”
Those final words matter.
His greeting was not simply a professional signature from a hired secretary.
It was a greeting expressed within the Christian relationship believers shared through Jesus Christ.
Whether Tertius was paid for his work, volunteered his service, or held some other role is not disclosed.
But his greeting places him within the Christian fellowship surrounding Paul.
He wasn't merely a hand holding a pen.
He was a person whose name and greeting were welcomed into the letter.
And suddenly, a quiet man becomes visible.
Think about the setting.
Romans was most likely written in the mid-to-late 50s AD, during Paul's time in Greece, probably in Corinth or its vicinity.

Romans 16:1–2 commends Phoebe, who was associated with the church at Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth. Romans 16:23 mentions Gaius and Erastus, names that also fit the broader Corinthian setting, although not every identification is certain.
Scholars generally understand the letter to have been written before Paul's journey to Jerusalem described in Romans 15:25–26.
We cannot reconstruct the exact room, the hour, or the appearance of Tertius.
Scripture does not tell us whether he was young or old, wealthy or poor, enslaved or free.
Some have speculated about his social standing because Tertius is a Latin name meaning “third,” and numbered names could be used among enslaved and formerly enslaved people.
But that does not prove his status.
We should never turn speculation into biblical biography.
Still, consider what we can reasonably picture.
A letter is being prepared.
Paul is communicating truths that have consumed his life since the risen Christ confronted him.
The message concerns the whole human race.
The guilt of humanity.
The holiness of God.
The righteousness revealed through faith.
The death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
The reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles.
The life of the Spirit.
The mercy of God.
And the transforming power of the Gospel.
Tertius is there, recording the words.
Perhaps he understood immediately how extraordinary the message was.
Perhaps some passages challenged him before they ever challenged Rome.
We don't know.
But imagine hearing this sentence as it was being committed to writing:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23 (KJV)
All.
Not merely the notorious sinner.
Not merely the corrupt official.
Not merely the violent criminal.
All.
The respected religious person.
The generous neighbor.
The person who smiles in public but carries bitterness in private.
The one who knows the language of worship but has quietly wandered away from God.
You.
Me.
Every human being who has ever needed mercy.
And then comes the breathtaking answer.
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 3:24 (KJV)
Freely.
By grace.
Through redemption.
In Christ Jesus.
Do you understand what that means?
God does not declare sinners righteous because they have finally become impressive enough to deserve His acceptance.
He justifies through the redeeming work of Jesus Christ.
The Greek word translated “freely” is δωρεάν (dōrean), carrying the sense of something given without payment by the recipient.
And χάρις (charis) means grace or favor.
This is not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
Paul himself confronts that distortion in Romans 6:1–2.
Grace is not God's agreement to leave us unchanged.
Grace is His undeserved favor that brings us to Christ, where forgiveness and a new life are found.
Maybe that is where this story becomes personal.
Because some of us have spent years trying to earn what Christ came to give.
We serve because we are terrified of disappointing God.
We give because we are afraid He will abandon us if we stop.
We smile because we don't want anyone to discover how exhausted we really are.
We call ourselves Christians, yet deep inside, we still behave as though the cross was not enough.
And Romans interrupts that exhausting performance.
It tells the truth about our sin.
Then it points us to a Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1 (KJV)
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα
Ouden ara nyn katakrima.
Literally, in its opening thought: “Therefore, now, no condemnation.”
The word κατάκριμα (katakrima) refers to condemnation, a judicial sentence against someone.
Paul is announcing the astonishing security of those who belong to Christ.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because judgment is imaginary.
Not because God has forgotten His holiness.
But because Jesus Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
And if you have been carrying the weight of yesterday's failures, hear this carefully.
Your past is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
Your shame is not more powerful than His resurrection.
Your history does not have the authority to overturn what God has accomplished through His Son.
But the promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not a blanket declaration that repentance and faith are unnecessary.
The same letter calls people to believe, confess Jesus as Lord, and live in the newness of life that follows union with Him.
This is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement with religious vocabulary.
Not motivational optimism decorated with Bible verses.
Not a transaction in which we purchase God's approval through our religious performance.
It is salvation by God's grace through Jesus Christ, received by faith, producing a life increasingly transformed by the Holy Spirit.
And here is the astonishing part.
The man who physically wrote down these truths is remembered in Scripture for doing something extraordinarily ordinary.
He wrote.
He served.
He contributed to the work entrusted to him.
No dramatic testimony is recorded.
No extraordinary title accompanies his name.
Just Tertius.
The one who wrote the letter.
There is something deeply comforting about that.
Because we live in a world obsessed with being seen.
We measure significance through attention.
We mistake recognition for usefulness.
We sometimes assume that if our names are not announced, our work must not matter.
And even in Christian ministry, that temptation can creep in.
We admire the preacher holding the microphone but overlook the person preparing the room.
We celebrate the missionary traveling across oceans but forget the believers who faithfully pray and give.
We notice the person whose testimony moves thousands but miss the quiet Christian sitting beside a grieving friend.
Yet the body of Christ was never designed to function through one visible person.
Paul explains this beautifully in 1 Corinthians 12.
Different members.
Different functions.
One body.
And the members that appear weaker are indispensable.
That is not a license to romanticize exploitation or demand that faithful people remain invisible.
It is a reminder that usefulness in God's kingdom is not measured by public applause.
Maybe you are a Tertius in somebody else's story.
You helped someone return to church, but nobody knows.
You sent a message at the exact moment a friend was losing hope.
You prayed for a child who still seems far from God.
You gave what you could to support the spread of the Gospel.
You shared a Scripture that someone read silently at midnight.
You encouraged a struggling believer who never told you how much your words mattered.
And sometimes you wonder whether any of it made a difference.
Listen.
We cannot promise that every unseen act will produce a spectacular earthly outcome.
Scripture does not promise that.
But Scripture does assure believers that faithful labor in the Lord is not empty.
“Forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.” — 1 Corinthians 15:58 (KJV)
That promise rests on the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because what matters is not whether the world remembers your name.
What matters is whether your life is being offered faithfully to the Lord.
Tertius gives us a remarkable glimpse of this truth.
Yet we must be careful not to make him the hero of a letter whose great subject is Jesus Christ.
Romans does not exist to celebrate the greatness of its scribe.
It exists to proclaim the Gospel of God concerning His Son.
And the Gospel is far greater than the person holding the pen.
Paul writes:
Not the power of a famous preacher.
Not the power of a gifted writer.
Not the power of a religious organization.
The power of God.
That is why the message can move through imperfect human servants without depending upon their greatness.
The servant may be forgotten.
The Gospel remains.
The messenger may die.
Christ lives.
The ink may fade.
The truth of God's Word endures.
And perhaps this is the most humbling thing about Tertius.
He was close enough to the writing of Romans to leave his greeting in its final chapter.
Yet his name never becomes the center of the story.
It is as though his brief appearance reminds us that God uses real people in the transmission of His Word, and then directs our eyes back to the Savior.
And isn't that what faithful Christian service should do?
Not make people dependent upon our personalities.
Not turn ministry into a monument to ourselves.
Not persuade people that supporting a human organization is the same thing as purchasing God's blessing.
But point them beyond us.
To Christ.
Always to Christ.
There is another detail in Romans that makes this even more beautiful.
Paul did not write as a man who believed he had no need of other believers.
The final chapter is filled with greetings, names, relationships, gratitude, and evidence of shared labor.
Phoebe.
Priscilla and Aquila.
Urbanus.
Tryphena and Tryphosa.
Persis.
Gaius.
Tertius.
These were not interchangeable decorations around Paul's ministry.
They were real people in the network of Christian fellowship and service.
Some labored at great personal cost.
Some opened their homes.
Some carried responsibilities we can only partly reconstruct.
And together, their presence reminds us that the spread of the Gospel has always involved more than the person standing at the front.
God works through His people.
Through voices.
Through hands.
Through hospitality.
Through generosity.
Through teaching.
Through encouragement.
Through writing.
Through sacrificial service.
And yes, through the ordinary believer who decides that the message of Jesus Christ is worth helping others hear.
That brings us to a question more important than whether your name will ever be remembered.
What are you doing with the Gospel that has been entrusted to you?
Not everyone is called to preach publicly.
Not everyone has the resources to finance a large ministry.
Not everyone can travel.
Not everyone can write.
Not everyone can teach.
But every Christian is called to belong to Christ and to live faithfully before Him.
Perhaps your contribution today is repentance.
Perhaps it is forgiving someone.
Perhaps it is returning to prayer after months of spiritual dryness.
Perhaps it is opening your Bible again.
Perhaps it is speaking honestly about the struggle you have hidden behind a carefully maintained smile.
Perhaps it is sharing the Gospel with someone you love.
And perhaps, for some, it is helping sustain a ministry that is committed to making biblical teaching and discipleship resources accessible to more people.
But before we talk about giving, we must remember something essential.
You cannot buy God's favor.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot replace repentance with financial support.
Jesus Christ has already paid the price of redemption.
Romans 3:24 calls justification a gift of grace.
Romans 5:8 reminds us that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Romans 10:9–13 points us toward faith in the risen Lord.
Our giving, therefore, must never be presented as the price of God's acceptance.
It can, however, become a sincere expression of gratitude and partnership in the Gospel.
Paul's teaching in 2 Corinthians 9:7 is clear:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
The same verse teaches that giving should not arise from reluctance or compulsion.
Not because heaven can be purchased.
Not because God needs your money.
But because the message of Jesus Christ deserves to be proclaimed faithfully, and those who have the means and desire can participate in that work.
Gospel Warrior exists to point people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
Our theme is not simply a memorable phrase.
That is the story of the Gospel.
Sin is real.
Shame is real.
Consequences are real.
But so is the mercy of God.
The cross does not pretend the scandal of human rebellion never happened.
It reveals how seriously God takes sin and how astonishingly He has acted to save sinners through His Son.
The resurrection declares that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And the Holy Spirit transforms believers into people who increasingly reflect their Savior.
That is the message we want more people to encounter.
The exhausted mother scrolling through Facebook after everyone else is asleep.
The father wondering whether his family can ever recover from the damage he caused.
The young person trapped between religious expectations and private temptation.
The believer who knows the language of worship but has forgotten the joy of walking with Jesus.
The person who has avoided church because they are ashamed of what others might discover.
The skeptic who has heard plenty about Christianity but very little about Christ Himself.
They do not need another performance.
They need the truth.
They need the Scriptures opened faithfully.
They need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is found in Jesus, and no one becomes too broken for the Gospel to call them home.
This is why your partnership can matter.
Supporting an online ministry should not replace responsibilities to your family, your local church, or others who depend on you.
Give wisely.
Give freely.
Give because you believe in the work.
And if you are unable to give financially, please understand this without any ambiguity:
You are no less welcome, no less valued, and no less loved by God.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Your presence in a community seeking to grow in Christ matters.
These are simply thank-you benefits, not spiritual rewards or promises of divine favor.
More Scripture.
More Christ-centered encouragement.
More biblical discipleship.
More opportunities to help people understand the Gospel.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration into deeper study, prayer, obedience, and spiritual maturity.
Because the goal is not merely to make someone feel something for thirty seconds.
The goal is to help people know Jesus Christ, understand His Word, and walk with Him when the emotions of the moment have passed.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen.
Someone may be convinced that their small acts of faithfulness are meaningless.
Someone may be serving quietly while fighting discouragement.
Someone may be struggling with guilt and desperately need to encounter the truth of Romans 8:1.
Someone may need to learn that salvation is not earned by religious performance but found through Jesus Christ.
And someone may discover this message because you chose to place it where they could read it.
For the day you wonder whether your prayers matter.
For the day you begin comparing your calling with someone else's platform.
Come back and remember the man who held the pen.
And I want to ask you something personal.
Not a question designed to make you look spiritual.
A question that invites honesty.
Have you ever felt like a Tertius—doing your best to serve God, yet wondering whether anyone notices?
Maybe you're still fighting.
Maybe you're exhausted.
Maybe you've been faithful in public while quietly falling apart in private.
Maybe you need someone to pray with you.
And if this story has reminded you that Christ can use ordinary people for His purposes, tell us about someone whose quiet faithfulness helped shape your life.
Your testimony might encourage another believer to keep going.
But please don't leave this article thinking the central lesson is simply that you should work harder for God.
That would miss the heart of Romans.
The heart of Romans is not that ordinary people can become extraordinary by trying harder.
The heart of Romans is that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
And from that reconciliation flows a transformed life.
Paul's letter eventually brings us to a magnificent appeal:
“I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” — Romans 12:1 (KJV)
Notice the order.
By the mercies of God.
Before the appeal to surrender comes the announcement of mercy.
Before the call to offer our lives comes the revelation of what God has done through Christ.
We do not surrender to make God merciful.
We surrender because His mercy has reached us.
We do not serve to purchase redemption.
We serve because redemption has changed us.
We do not give to earn salvation.
We give, when able and willing, as one expression of love and gratitude.
And we do not seek recognition as the ultimate reward of faithfulness.
We seek to honor the Lord who first loved us.
Tertius wrote down the letter.
Paul delivered the apostolic message.
But the Savior proclaimed throughout Romans is Jesus Christ.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One in whom there is no condemnation for those who belong to Him.
The One who calls us to repentance, faith, and a new life.
And perhaps, when you open your Bible tonight and read Romans again, you will notice something you missed before.
At the end of a letter that has transformed countless lives, a man briefly introduces himself.
“I Tertius…”
Then he steps back into history.
We are not told what happened to him afterward.
We do not know how long he lived.
We do not know whether he ever imagined that believers nearly two thousand years later would still be reading his name.
And we should not pretend to know what Scripture has left unsaid.
But we do know that his service became part of the history of a letter through which generations have encountered the Gospel.
That is enough to make us grateful.
Not because Tertius was the redeemer.
But because his quiet contribution directs our attention toward the Redeemer.
So tonight, if you feel forgotten, remember that your worth is not determined by the number of people who know your name.
If you feel ashamed, turn to the Christ who receives repentant sinners.
If you feel exhausted, remember that God's grace is not a wage paid to the impressive.
If you feel unqualified, remember that the church is a body of many members, each called to serve according to the gifts and opportunities God provides.
And if you have spent your life trying to prove that you deserve to be loved by God, stop looking to your achievements for the assurance only Christ can give.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Let His Word expose what needs to change.
Let His grace lead you away from sin.
Let His mercy humble you.
Let His resurrection give you hope.
And let your life, whether public or hidden, become an offering of gratitude to the One who saved you.
Because the greatest miracle in the story of Romans is not that a forgotten man held the pen.
It is that the God who is perfectly holy made a way for guilty sinners to be forgiven and brought near through Jesus Christ.
And the greatest thing about your story will never be how many people remember you.
It will be whether your life points them toward Him.
The world may never remember the hands that carried the message—but heaven's greatest treasure is the Savior that message reveals.
